# [An Introduction to Digital Filters, without the mathematics](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qmd685msY-Y)

**Visibility**: Public
**Uploaded by**: [Akash Murthy](http://www.youtube.com/@akashmurthy)
**Uploaded at**: 2022-11-24T01:37:36-08:00
**Published at**: 2022-11-24T01:37:36-08:00
**Length**: 04:55
**Views**: 43276
**Likes**: 1142
**Category**: Science & Technology

## Description

```
In this series on Digital Filter Basics, we'll take a slow and cemented dive into the fascinating world of digital filter theory. Many resources present this topic with dense and exhausting mathematics. Although a fair understanding of complex mathematics is required to fully comprehend the science of filter design, understanding the basics of filters and how they fundamentally work is better left to analysis and visualizations, which I try to do in this series. 

Find the full playlist here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qmd685msY-Y&list=PLbqhA-NKGP6Afr_KbPUuy_yIBpPR4jzWo

References:
Designing Audio Effect Plugins in C++, Will C. Pirkle - 
https://www.willpirkle.com/about/books/
Introduction to Digital Filters, Julius O. Smith - https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/

If you've got any questions, suggestions or recommendations, type them out here, or send me a message on any of my social channels mentioned below. 

A lot of time was spent on creating this series, and I plan to do more. So please consider subscribing if you wish to be notified about more releases in the future. And if you feel generous: https://www.patreon.com/akashmurthy

Check out my music here: https://farfetchd-official.bandcamp.com/

Check out the audio track in the intro and outro here: https://soundcloud.com/thrifleganger/tinderbox

Give me a shout here: 
Website - https://www.akashmurthy.com/
Facebook - https://www.facebook.com/akash.murthy.319
Instagram - https://www.instagram.com/thrifleganger/
```

## Transcript

Digital Signal   Processing, and for us audiophiles and musicians, 
Audio Signal Processing is a fascinating area of   study. In it, encompasses all of the audio effects 
that we know and love, including filters, delays,   reverbs, modulators, dynamic processors like 
compressors, and limiters, non linear processors   like distortion and saturation, phase vocoders, 
pitch shifters and all the others in between   I’ve failed to mention. And what many books 
and resources on these topics fail to mention   is that mathematics is complex. Not necessarily 
complicated, but a fundamental understanding of   complex numbers and complex algebra is required 
to understand a wide variety of textbooks related   to the discussion of DSP. And once you get into 
them, you realize that it doesn’t just end there,   you need to understand complex sinusoids, Z 
transforms and Fourier transforms which convert   discrete or continuous time complex signals 
into their frequency domain representations,   and a healthy understanding of trigonometry, 
vector geometry and calculus. And that’s when we   choose to close the book, and fend off an eternal 
sense of dread and insecurity. I’ve been there.   For a lot of people getting into DSP has a high 
barrier for entry. And don’t get me wrong, I’m   not dissing any of the books for being extremely 
pedantic. It can be quite complicated if you get   into the nitty gritty, but from a distance, it 
doesn’t have to be. Intuitively understanding   these subjects irrespective of the math is the 
most sure fire way of building foundational   understanding and interest in the subject. 
And once you develop interest and once you So, this entire series is dedicated to the 
discussion of one of the core areas of DSP   and an effect that’s widely used in every 
realm of audio processing - filters. We’ll   approach filtering with as little 
complex mathematics as possible,   and rather rely on an analytical approach 
of simulations and visualizations to   get an intimate understanding of 
filters, how they work and behave. This section is heavily borrowed from the amazing   work put in by Will Pirkle in his book 
Designing Audio Effect Plugins in C++.   If you haven’t already checked it 
out, I’d encourage you to do so. So, let’s see what we’d be covering in this 
series. We’ll start with what a filter is and the   terminologies used to describe the characteristics 
of a filter. We’ll look at a couple of ways of   analyzing the result or the response of a filter 
by looking at frequency and phase response graphs.   Then we’ll take a quick stab at the different 
types of input signals that we may want to   experiment with. These aren’t going to be audio 
signals as such, but really simple test signals   that we can step through sample by sample and 
understand how a filter might process them.   We’ll look at the simple building blocks of any 
filter design including delays, amps and summing   mixers, and view them as structural black 
boxes that we can arrange in a flow diagram.   We’ll look at the simplest filter topology - 
a first order feed forward low pass filter.   We’ll run through the test signals through 
this theoretical filter, going over the signal,   step by step, sample by sample to see 
how the filter processes the test signal.   Through this, we’ll discover the fundamental 
principles on how a filter attenuates or boosts   certain frequency within a signal. We’ll look at 
why this filter is also called a finite impulse   response filter, or an FIR filter, and how FIR 
filters can maintain linear phase characteristics.  After that, we’ll look at a simple modification of 
this topology to get a 1st order feedback filter,   and we’ll do the same analysis with 
this. We’ll see how an introduction   of a feedback loop into the topology 
creates a starkly different response.   And we’ll see why this type of filter is called an 
infinite impulse response filter or an IIR filter. Finally, we’ll look at a few code examples 
in Python which will help us solidify the   concepts and a JUCE plugin which implements 
these simple designs and try them out on some   real world audio signals. This will be a lot of 
fun, since we’ll be building a filter algorithm   in C++ with barely any mathematics at its core. 
Because of this, we don't use conventional filter   inputs - like cutoff frequency, bandwidth or Q, 
or gain controls. All we expose is a couple of   coefficients that we can control and it’s fun 
to see how changing them will result in really   unpredictable behavior in the filter response 
and ponder upon why it behaves the way it does. So, with that introduction out 
of the way, let’s get started.

> # Digital Filter Theory Summary
>
> This section summarizes [digital filter theory](https://technick.net/guides/theory/dft/introduction_digital_filter) in a rather terse
> fashion suitable for review study. _linearity_, _time-invariance_ and four basic representations of [digital\\
> filters](http://www.dsptutor.freeuk.com/dfilt1.php) are defined: the _[difference equation](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/difference_equation.php) coefficients, [impulse response](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/difference_equation.php#2324), transfer function,_ and _[frequency response](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/frequency_response.php)_.
> Next the concepts of _[phase delay](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/phase_delay_group.php)_ and _[group delay](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/phase_delay_group.php)_ are
> defined. This material is a subset of that in \[ [1](https://technick.net/guides/theory/dft/bibliography#JOSFP)\].
>
> **Definition.** A real _signal_ is defined as any real-valued function
> of the integers. Similarly a complex signal is any complex-valued
> function of the integers.
>
> **Definition.** A real _[filter](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos//filters/difference_equation.php)_![${\](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img1555.png) is defined as any
> real-valued [functional](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/functional.php) of a signal for each integer ![$n$](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img51.png). We express
> the input-output relation of the filter by
>
> ![\](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img1556.png)
>
> where ![$x(\](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img44.png) is the entire input signal, and ![$y(n)$](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img641.png) is the output
> at time ![$n$](https://technick.net/img/guide_dft/img51.png).
